facts.claim: "Bad For Me" is track 3 on Peter Raffoul's six-song EP Songs from House In Blue, released July 1, 2022.
Raffoul co-wrote "Bad For Me" with Connor Thuotte and Kate York.

Credits list Owen Lewis as producer and programmer, Connor Thuotte on guitar, and Raffoul on piano. Chris Gehringer, John O'Mahony and Henry Brill also appear in the production and engineering credits.
The EP's press notes describe the song as bringing potent beats and prismatic textures to an unflinching meditation on cycles of self-destruction.
Raffoul said that during a breakup or other hard time, doing things that are bad for you can feel easier as a way to numb yourself. This is the idea the song grew from.
Raffoul said Thuotte played a simple chord progression on a $5 yard-sale guitar, and that guitar part was used on the final version.
Official music video, lyric video and rooftop performance videos of "Bad For Me" were released on YouTube.
Raffoul is a Canadian-born, Nashville-based singer-songwriter from Leamington, Ontario. Songs from House In Blue was his debut EP.
He comes from a musical family: his father Jody has played in rock bands for over three decades, and his brother Billy is a singer-songwriter signed to Interscope. Peter took up piano at 17.
Raffoul has said most of his songs are about admitting that things are far from perfect, and that he finds hopefulness in that.

research.lineage: Raffoul's Nashville-based alternative singer-songwriter music mixes raw, confessional songwriting with influences from the Beatles, late-'80s college rock, left-of-center hip-hop and soulful balladry.

draft:
The phrase that matters most in **Bad For Me** is the one that doesn't finish. Again and again the chorus reaches for its reason, "to make me feel better," and on the fourth pass it stops short: "To make me feel." The word "better" just falls away. It's a small cut, but it changes the whole confession. The narrator isn't chasing happiness anymore. They're chasing any feeling at all, and the song keeps landing on that gap until it ends there, still unfinished.

Peter Raffoul built the song from a plain idea he's described in interviews. When you're going through a breakup or some other hard stretch, doing what's bad for you can feel easier, because it numbs you. The verses spell out the trap without excuses: weeks of getting high and staying numb, places you shouldn't be, and the flat admission that "something / Always seems to feel like nothing." That line holds the real ache. The trouble isn't that nothing helps. It's that even the things that should help feel like nothing.

The second verse names what the numbness is covering. The narrator pictures someone else holding an ex and telling them the same things they once heard, then asks the question underneath everything: "Or am I in this alone." Self-destruction sits right next to a stubborn, almost hopeful need to know the other person hurts too. The song doesn't pretend that need is noble, and it doesn't settle it either.

The sound stays gentle where a lesser song might lean on drama. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through arpeggios. Raffoul has said co-writer Connor Thuotte played that simple progression on a $5 yard-sale guitar, and the part made the final cut. Bass holds sustained root notes, and a slow kick and snare join without hurry, the arrangement stacking up one patient layer at a time. Raffoul's voice is mid-range with a little rasp, sustained and steady with a light vibrato, sometimes shadowed by a softer harmony above. Owen Lewis's production is clean and dry, so nothing blurs the words.

Raffoul, a Leamington, Ontario native working out of Nashville, wrote it with Thuotte and Kate York for his debut EP, *Songs from House In Blue*. It fits the confessional, soul-leaning balladry he draws on, and his own description of his songs, admitting things are far from perfect and finding a kind of hope in saying so. The hope here is in the honesty itself.

That clipped "to make me feel" is the hook that stays with you, because it catches the exact moment when wanting to feel better gives way to just wanting to feel anything.
